slides.title: How Many Patients to Treat for One Benefit
bullets: Number needed to treat, NNT, is how many patients must be treated for one to avoid the event, versus control
Number needed to harm, NNH, is how many must be treated for one additional adverse effect
Both translate trial results into a practical, bedside decision

slides.title: NNT Is the Inverse of Absolute Risk Reduction
bullets: NNT equals 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction between control and treated event rates
This makes NNT highly sensitive to the population's baseline risk
The same relative risk can produce very different NNTs depending on baseline event frequency

slides.title: Low NNT Means an Efficient Treatment

stats.label: real benefit, but diluted across many patients

slides.caption: The same statistically significant benefit can look very different in practice.

slides.title: Absolute Effect in Plain Language
bullets: NNT communicates absolute effect size in language any clinician can interpret directly
Relative measures like RR or HR can make a small absolute benefit sound bigger than it is
Current guidance recommends reporting NNT and NNH alongside relative measures, especially for non-specialists

slides.title: NNT Doesn't Travel Well
bullets: It's only valid for the follow-up period of the original study
It's specific to the population studied, so a very different baseline risk can mislead
As a population average, it says nothing about one individual patient's probability of benefit

slides.title: Balance Benefit Against Harm
bullets: Present the NNT of the main benefit alongside the NNH of the most relevant adverse effect
This lets the HCP see both sides of the risk-benefit balance in the same numeric language
That balanced framing makes a genuinely informed conversation with the patient possible

takeaway.title: NNT and NNH turn statistics into a bedside risk-benefit conversation
bullets: NNT is the inverse of absolute risk reduction, and depends heavily on baseline risk
A low NNT means an efficient treatment, a high NNT means a diluted benefit
Pairing NNT with NNH gives an HCP both sides of the risk-benefit balance
